extracted.intended_audience: law students, patent attorneys, and judges (patent practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on assessing novelty, prior use, abandonment, and what constitutes a completed invention for patent validity; focuses on factual questions courts/juries must decide and statutory limits on prior knowledge. Draws on case examples (spent madder, Booth v. Kennard, Fitzgerald/Conner).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable character as question of fact
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentable character of the invention is a question of fact for the jury and should not be treated as an inference of law drawn from too narrow a basis of facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A trial court must direct the jury to find specific factual questions (e.g., chemical differences between substances, whether prior processes were applied to new substances) rather than tell the jury to deem patentability as a legal inference. (Example: Steiner v. Heald — jury should have been directed to find certain factual questions.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality and extent of difference from prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty depends on the quality and extent of the difference between the alleged invention and things which preceded it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An invention may be invalid if it is merely a double use of an old process; conversely, even a subtle but material difference can support a patent. Courts analyze how substantially the new thing differs from prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of an old process to a new substance may be inventive
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying an old contrivance or process to a new subject-matter can constitute an invention if the new subject-matter is substantially different from the old one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: spent madder vs fresh madder — if spent madder is chemically or otherwise substantially different, applying the old extraction process to it could be an invention; if it is substantially the same, it may be mere repetition of an old process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission of a process step can be an invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The omission (saving) of a step in an existing process may be a substantive invention capable of supporting a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Booth v. Kennard — making gas directly from seeds by omitting a previous extraction step was held a substantive invention even though apparatus and resulting gas were the same.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory novelty requirement (not known or used by others)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the statute the subject-matter sought must be 'not known or used by others before his or their discovery or invention thereof.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory language raises questions about timing (time of invention vs time of application) and whose knowledge counts. The treatise explains the historical construction (public possession before application defeats patent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public possession/use before application defeats patent
rubrics_metrics.description: If the public were in possession of the invention at the time of the application, whether derived from another inventor or the applicant himself with consent, the patent is invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Supreme Court construed the statute to mean 'not known or used by the public before the application.' Prior private or secret uses not accessible to the public do not automatically defeat the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior use by others (one person) can defeat novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior use or knowledge by any other person (not the applicant) is sufficient to defeat a claim of being the inventor, unless excluded by other statutory limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term 'others' in the statute was intended to mean any person other than the patentee; a single prior user can be enough if the use/knowledge was in a manner accessible to the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign prior use/patent/publication limitation (15th section)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patentee believed himself to be the first inventor, the invention is not void for having been known or used in a foreign country provided it has not been previously patented or described in any printed publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This protects reinvention in the U.S. of unpatented/unpublished foreign inventions or 'lost' foreign arts because the public here had no reasonable means to obtain the foreign knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost or abandoned prior inventions do not bar later patents
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior invention which has been finally forgotten, abandoned, or lost (so that no existing and living knowledge of it exists) does not prevent a subsequent independent inventor from obtaining a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases (e.g., Fitzgerald/Conner) required juries to find whether the earlier device had been finally forgotten or abandoned; if so, the later inventor who rediscovers it by his own efforts may be entitled to a patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secret or concealed prior use may be treated as abandoned/lost
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior machines kept locked, concealed, or known only to a few persons and not accessible to the public may be treated as substantially abandoned or lost so as not to bar a later patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a machine kept under lock in a cellar known only to the maker and close relatives, neglected and rusty, may be considered absent from public knowledge; courts considered whether public could derive benefit from it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completed invention (reduced to practice) required to defeat later patent
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not sufficient that another previously conceived the idea; he must have reduced it to practice and embodied it in a useful practical form to defeat a later patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drawings or mere representations are not enough. The prior device/experiment must have been brought to a practical, completed form capable of producing a useful result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior experiments do not invalidate a subsequent completed invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior experiments, not brought to a practical completed form, will not invalidate a later invention that completes the idea into a working device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior machines must have been working machines (actually done work or capable of doing it) rather than mere experiments to be effective prior art against a later patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural inventions may be complete without public testing
rubrics_metrics.description: For inventions that are mere structures whose adaptation or capacity requires no practical test, prior making of the structure (even without use) may be sufficient to show a completed prior invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In such cases (rare), proof that the prior structure was actually made may invalidate a later patent even if there was no public use or testing (example: certain water-wheel cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inquiry focuses on whether results are substantially the same in kind
rubrics_metrics.description: The true inquiry is not questions of degree or perfection but whether the two things actually accomplished a result that may be regarded as substantially the same in kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence about expert opinions on whether a prior machine 'would have worked' is only relevant insofar as it aids the inference that the prior thing actually worked; courts avoid getting lost in degrees of perfection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jury must be instructed to find key factual predicates (abandonment, originality, substance difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts should instruct juries to find factual predicates such as whether a prior thing was finally forgotten/abandoned, whether the later inventor was original, and whether substances/process applications were substantially different.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper jury directions are essential (e.g., require findings on whether spent madder differs chemically from fresh madder; whether Conner's safe had been forgotten) because these facts materially affect validity.
